title: Government Bonds
intro: Bonds issued by national governments in their own currency are the closest thing to a risk-free asset, because such a government can always create the money to pay. Their yields are the base rate against which everything else is priced. This page covers the main markets, the special kinds of government bond, and municipal bonds.

blocks.text: Why they are 'risk-free', and when they are not

A government that borrows in a currency it issues itself cannot be forced into default by lack of money, though it can choose to default for political reasons, and it can inflate the debt away. So for these bonds the main risks are interest-rate risk and inflation, not default. Governments that borrow in a currency they do not control are different: euro-area countries depend on the European Central Bank, and many emerging markets borrow in dollars. Greece restructured its debt in 2012 with large losses for bondholders; Argentina has defaulted many times; Russia defaulted on ruble debt in 1998.

items: Treasury bills (T-bills): zero-coupon, maturities of 4 to 52 weeks. The usual measure of the risk-free rate and what money market funds hold.
Treasury notes: 2, 3, 5, 7 and 10 years, coupons twice a year. The 10-year Treasury yield is the most-watched rate in the world; mortgage rates follow it.

TIPS (Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities): the principal rises with US CPI, and the fixed coupon is paid on the adjusted principal, so you get a known real yield. At maturity you get at least the original face.

Series I savings bonds: sold directly to individuals with yearly purchase limits; their rate combines a fixed rate and an inflation rate, they can't lose value, and they can't be sold to others; they can't be cashed for a year, and cashing before five years costs three months' interest.
Floating rate notes: coupons reset with T-bill rates.

blocks.text: Treasuries are bought at auction (TreasuryDirect lets individuals buy directly) and trade in the deepest, most liquid bond market in the world, roughly \$28 trillion of marketable debt in 2025. Interest is taxed federally but exempt from US state and local income tax.

The difference between a nominal Treasury yield and the TIPS yield of the same maturity is the breakeven inflation rate: the average inflation at which the two give the same return. If the 10-year Treasury yields 4.3% and the 10-year TIPS yields 2.0%, breakeven is about 2.3%. Buy TIPS if you expect inflation above that (or want insurance against it); nominal bonds if below. Breakevens are a widely used market forecast of inflation, though they also include a risk premium and liquidity effects.

items: United Kingdom: gilts. Conventional gilts and index-linked gilts (linked to RPI historically, moving toward CPIH from 2030). The UK's 2022 'mini-budget' crisis, when long gilt yields jumped over a point in days and pension funds using leveraged liability-driven investment faced collateral calls, is a modern lesson in duration and leverage.
Germany: Bunds (Bundesanleihen). The benchmark for the euro area; other euro governments are quoted by their spread over Bunds (the Italy-Germany spread is a gauge of euro stress).
Other euro governments: France (OATs), Italy (BTPs), Spain (Bonos) and others. Same currency, different credit risk.

Japan: JGBs. Japan has government debt over 200% of GDP, mostly owned at home and by the Bank of Japan, which held 10-year yields near zero under 'yield curve control' from 2016 and has been letting them rise since 2024.
Canada, Australia, Switzerland and the Nordic countries: high-rated, smaller markets.
China: a large onshore government bond market, now in global indexes, with capital controls.

Emerging-market sovereigns: issued both in local currency (higher yields with currency risk) and in dollars or euros (credit risk without currency risk to a dollar investor). The JP Morgan EMBI and GBI-EM indexes track them.
US agency debt: issued by government-sponsored enterprises such as Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and the Federal Home Loan Banks; slightly higher yield than Treasuries.
Mortgage-backed securities (MBS): pools of home loans, most guaranteed by Ginnie Mae (explicitly by the US government) or Fannie and Freddie. Homeowners can prepay, so MBS have negative convexity.
Supranationals: the World Bank, the European Investment Bank and others; very high quality.

Municipal bonds (munis): issued by US states, cities and agencies. Interest is usually exempt from federal income tax (and from state tax for residents of the issuing state). General obligation bonds are backed by taxing power; revenue bonds by a specific project's income (a toll road, an airport). Defaults are rare but happen (Detroit 2013, Puerto Rico 2016-17).

A 3.5% muni for an investor in the 35% bracket is worth $3.5/0.65 \approx 5.4\%$ taxable. For someone in the 12% bracket it is worth only about 4.0%, so munis mostly suit high-income investors in taxable accounts, and never belong in an IRA.

For money you need in the next year or two: T-bills, government money market funds, short Treasury ETFs, and bank deposits and CDs (in the US, FDIC-insured to \$250,000 per depositor per bank per ownership category). Their yields follow the central bank's policy rate closely.

blocks.title: Breakeven
blocks.text: A 5-year Treasury yields 4.0% and a 5-year TIPS yields 1.6%. What inflation rate makes them equal? If you expect 3% inflation, which do you prefer?
solution: At 3% inflation TIPS return about $1.6 + 3 = 4.6\%$ nominal, more than 4.0%. Prefer TIPS.

blocks.title: Muni or taxable
blocks.text: You are in the 32% federal bracket and live in a state with no income tax. A muni yields 3.4%; a corporate bond of similar quality and maturity yields 4.8%. Which pays more after tax?
solution: Tax-equivalent yield of the muni $= 3.4/0.68 = 5.0\%$, above 4.8%. Equivalently, the corporate's after-tax yield is $4.8 \times 0.68 = 3.26\%$, below 3.4%. The muni pays more.

blocks.title: TIPS mechanics
blocks.text: You buy \$10,000 face of a TIPS with a 1.5% coupon. Over the first year CPI rises 4%. What is the adjusted principal, and what interest do you receive for the year (ignoring the timing within the year)?
solution: Principal $= 10000 \times 1.04 = \$10{,}400$. Interest $\approx 1.5\% \times 10400 = \$156$. Both the principal and the interest have kept pace with prices; in the US the \$400 principal increase is taxable that year even though you don't receive it in cash, which is why TIPS fit best in tax-advantaged accounts.
